GCC compiles this without a word of complaint, because a declaration is all a call needs to be well formed, and fails only at the link step, where

A multiple definition is the opposite shape and cannot happen in one file.

files, each one pastes a full copy of that definition into its own translation unit, and each translation unit compiles to an object file that exports its own

external symbol, and it refuses to guess which one is real.

You pass if the program you wrote fails at the link step with exactly this message, not a compiler error, and if the explanation names two separate translation units as the reason a multiple definition needs more than one file. Saying only "there are two of the same function" without saying they come from separate
files compiling the same header is a partial pass. Confusing either error for a compile error, one that stops before an object file exists, is a fail.
Building a C++ program has two jobs split across two tools. The compiler turns one
file, after the preprocessor has pasted in every header it
s, into one object file: this expanded, self-contained unit of source is a

, and the compiler only ever sees one at a time. The linker then takes every object file the program needs and produces one executable, resolving every name one translation unit merely declared against the one place some translation unit defined it.
The problem this split creates is that a translation unit calling a function only needs to see its
, the name and its type; it does not need the
, the body, which may live in another file entirely. That is what makes separate compilation possible at all: change one

file and only it needs recompiling, as long as the declarations everyone else saw have not changed. It is also where both of this topic's errors live. A name declared and called but never defined anywhere the linker looks is an
. A name given an ordinary definition in more than one translation unit, most often because that definition sat in a header two
: the one-definition rule allows exactly one, and the linker enforces it for anything without internal or

The mechanism behind both is the object file's symbol table: every name a translation unit defines is exported from it, and every name it uses but does not define is left for the linker to find, undefined, in some other object file or library.

changes what counts as one definition: the same inline function may be defined in every translation unit that includes its header, because the standard allows it, as long as every copy is token-for-token identical, and the linker keeps exactly one of them.
What it costs is that a violation the compiler and linker cannot see does not stop the build at all: two translation units defining the same
function differently both compile and link without complaint, and the program runs anyway, wrong in a way that shifts with how hard the compiler was told to optimise.
You meet this in every project split across more than one
file, and the interview question is exactly the pair a linker actually reports: too few definitions, or too many.

at all. Nothing here is a link error, because the symbol
exists on both sides and its mangled name did not change; the
the two sides agree the argument has did change, silently, which is what an
is: two separately compiled pieces that still link because their names match, disagreeing about what those names mean in memory. The Itanium C++ ABI (

), which GCC and Clang both implement on Linux, is the specification that fixes struct layout, name mangling and calling convention well enough that separately compiled object files can be linked at all; it says nothing about whether two versions of your own header still agree, because that promise is yours to keep, not the compiler's. A header shipped to other translation units, or across a shared library boundary, keeps that promise only if every consumer is rebuilt whenever it changes, which is why a public C++ library that must stay binary-compatible hides layout changes behind a pointer that never changes size, and recompiles everything else from source.
